For f to be **continuous at x = 2**, the limit as x → 2 must exist **and** equal f(2) = 2.
**Step 1 — see why the numerator must vanish.** As x → 2 the denominator x − 2 tends to 0.
If the numerator tended to anything other than 0, the quotient would blow up and no finite
limit could exist. So we need
**N(2) = 0**, where N(x) = x² − (a + 2)x + a
**Step 2 — impose it.**
2² − (a + 2)(2) + a = 0
4 − 2a − 4 + a = 0
**−a = 0**
**a = 0**
**Step 3 — check the limit then comes out right.** With a = 0 the function is
f(x) = (x² − 2x)/(x − 2) = x(x − 2)/(x − 2) = **x** for x ≠ 2
so
lim(x→2) f(x) = **2**
and f(2) = **2** ✓ The two agree, so f is continuous at x = 2 and a = 0 is confirmed ✓
**Why the 0/0 form had to be arranged.** A removable discontinuity is the only way a
quotient with a vanishing denominator can be patched. Forcing the numerator to vanish too
makes (x − 2) a **common factor**, and cancelling it leaves a function that is perfectly
well behaved at x = 2.
**What the other values of a would do.** Take a = 1, for instance:
N(x) = x² − 3x + 1 and N(2) = 4 − 6 + 1 = **−1 ≠ 0**
so f(x) → −1/0, which is unbounded — the function has an **infinite** discontinuity at
x = 2 and no value of f(2) could repair it ✗ The same happens for a = −1 and a = −6: only
a = 0 makes the numerator vanish.
**A neat way to see it.** For (x − 2) to be a factor of the numerator, the numerator must
be (x − 2) times something, and that something must be (x − a) to give the right sum of
roots. Multiplying out,
(x − a)(x − 2) = x² − (a + 2)x + **2a**
while the numerator given is x² − (a + 2)x + **a**. The x² and x terms already agree, and
the constants agree only when 2a = a, that is **a = 0** ✓ the same condition, found by
factorising rather than substituting.
∴ 0.

The **mean value theorem** says that for a function continuous on [a, b] and differentiable
on (a, b) there is some c in (a, b) with
**f′(c) = [f(b) − f(a)]/(b − a)**
— a point where the tangent is parallel to the chord.
**Step 1 — check the hypotheses.** f(x) = x² is a polynomial, so it is continuous on [2, 4]
and differentiable on (2, 4) ✓ The theorem applies.
**Step 2 — compute the right-hand side**, the gradient of the chord.
f(4) = 4² = **16**
f(2) = 2² = **4**
[f(4) − f(2)]/(4 − 2) = (16 − 4)/2 = 12/2 = **6**
**Step 3 — differentiate.**
f′(x) = **2x**
**Step 4 — solve f′(c) = 6.**
2c = 6
**c = 3** ✓
**Step 5 — check c lies strictly inside the interval.** 2 < 3 < 4 ✓ as the theorem
requires. (A value landing on an endpoint would mean an error somewhere, since the theorem
guarantees an **interior** point.)
**Verifying geometrically.** The chord joins (2, 4) to (4, 16), with gradient 6. The
tangent to y = x² at x = 3 touches at (3, 9) and has gradient 2(3) = **6** ✓ The two lines
are parallel, which is exactly what the theorem promises.
**A pattern worth noticing.** For f(x) = x² on any interval [a, b],
f′(c) = (b² − a²)/(b − a) = **a + b**, and 2c = a + b, so **c = (a + b)/2**
The mean value point of a parabola is always the **midpoint** of the interval. Here
(2 + 4)/2 = **3** ✓ — the answer in one step, with no differentiation at all.
**Why the other options fail.** c = 2 and c = 4 are the **endpoints**, which the theorem
excludes; and c = 7/2 = 3·5 would give f′(3·5) = 7, not 6 ✗
∴ 3.

Multiplying a matrix by a scalar multiplies **every** entry, and the determinant picks up
one factor of that scalar from **each row**.
**Step 1 — state the rule.** For an n × n matrix A and a scalar K,
**|KA| = Kⁿ |A|**
**Step 2 — apply it with n = 3.**
**|KA| = K³ |A|** ✓
**Why the exponent is n and not 1.** A determinant is a sum of products, each containing
exactly **one entry from every row**. Scaling the matrix by K scales each of those n
entries by K, so each product gains a factor Kⁿ, and so does the whole determinant. For a
3 × 3 matrix that is K³.
**A worked check.** Take the identity matrix I₃, whose determinant is 1. Then KI₃ is the
diagonal matrix with K, K, K down the diagonal, and its determinant is
K × K × K = **K³** = K³ × 1 ✓
Another: let A = [[1, 0, 0], [0, 2, 0], [0, 0, 3]], so |A| = 6. Then 2A has diagonal
2, 4, 6 and determinant 2 × 4 × 6 = **48** = 2³ × 6 ✓
**The row-by-row view.** Pulling a common factor K out of **one** row multiplies the
determinant by K. A 3 × 3 matrix has three rows, each carrying a factor K, so three factors
come out:
|KA| = K · K · K · |A| = **K³|A|** ✓
**Why the distractors are tempting.** **K|A|** is what would happen if only one row were
scaled; **3K|A|** confuses multiplying by K three times with adding it three times; and
**K²|A|** is the rule for a 2 × 2 matrix. Each is correct for a different situation, and
only K³|A| is right for order 3.
**A contrast worth remembering.** For the **adjugate** of a 3 × 3 matrix the rule is
|adj A| = |A|², and for the inverse |A⁻¹| = 1/|A|. These exponents are easy to mix up, and
each has to be read off from its own definition.
∴ K³|A|.

The question asks which statement is **not** correct, so each must be checked against the
standard results for invertible matrices.
**Statement (2): A(adj A) = (adj A)A = |A| I** ✓ **TRUE**
This is the defining property of the **adjugate** (adjoint). Expanding any row of A against
its own cofactors gives |A|, while expanding it against **another** row's cofactors gives 0
— so the product is |A| on the diagonal and 0 everywhere else, which is precisely |A| I.
**Statement (1): A(adj A) = (adj A)A = A I** ✗ **FALSE**
The right-hand side should be **|A| I**, a scalar multiple of the identity, not **A I**.
Note that A I = A, so statement (1) is claiming A(adj A) = A, which would force
adj A = I for every invertible A — plainly untrue.
**A 2 × 2 counter-example.** Take A = [[1, 2], [3, 4]], with |A| = 4 − 6 = **−2** and
adj A = [[4, −2], [−3, 1]]. Then
A(adj A) = [[1(4) + 2(−3), 1(−2) + 2(1)], [3(4) + 4(−3), 3(−2) + 4(1)]]
= [[4 − 6, −2 + 2], [12 − 12, −6 + 4]]
= [[−2, 0], [0, −2]]
= **−2 I = |A| I** ✓ matching statement (2)
But A I = A = [[1, 2], [3, 4]], which is **not** [[−2, 0], [0, −2]] ✗ so statement (1)
fails.
**Statement (3): (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹** ✓ **TRUE** — the **reversal law**. Checking:
(AB)(B⁻¹A⁻¹) = A(BB⁻¹)A⁻¹ = A I A⁻¹ = AA⁻¹ = I ✓
The order **must** reverse, because matrix multiplication does not commute.
**Statement (4): |A| ≠ 0, |B| ≠ 0** ✓ **TRUE** — this is exactly what being invertible
means, since A⁻¹ = (adj A)/|A| requires a non-zero denominator.
**The one word that decides it.** Statement (1) differs from statement (2) by a single
symbol, **A** where **|A|** belongs. One is a matrix, the other a scalar, and the adjugate
identity produces a scalar multiple of the identity — never the matrix A itself.
∴ A(adj A) = (adj A)A = AI is the incorrect statement.

Again the task is to find the statement that is **not** correct, among four determinant
properties for invertible n × n matrices.
**Statement (1): det(AB) = det(A) · det(B)** ✓ **TRUE**
This is the **multiplicative property** of determinants, and it is one of the most useful
facts about them. It is also why |A| ≠ 0 is preserved under multiplication.
**Statement (2): det(kA) = kⁿ det(A)** ✓ **TRUE**
Scaling the matrix by k scales every one of the n rows by k, and each row contributes one
factor, so kⁿ comes out in all.
**Statement (3): det(A + B) = det(A) + det(B)** ✗ **FALSE**
The determinant is **not additive**. It is a multilinear function of the rows, not a linear
function of the matrix.
**A counter-example in the simplest case.** Take A = B = I₂, so that
det(A) = det(B) = **1**
A + B = 2I₂, whose determinant is 2 × 2 = **4**
But det(A) + det(B) = 1 + 1 = **2** ✗ and 4 ≠ 2, so the statement fails ✓
A second, even starker example: let A = [[1, 0], [0, 0]] and B = [[0, 0], [0, 1]]. Then
det(A) = det(B) = **0**, yet A + B = I₂ with det = **1** ≠ 0 + 0 ✗
**Statement (4): det(A′) = 1/det(A⁻¹)** ✓ **TRUE**
Since AA⁻¹ = I, taking determinants gives det(A)·det(A⁻¹) = 1, so
det(A⁻¹) = 1/det(A), and therefore 1/det(A⁻¹) = **det(A)** ✓
And det(A′) = det(A), because transposing a matrix leaves its determinant unchanged. So
both sides equal det(A) ✓
**The pattern across the four.** The determinant behaves beautifully under **multiplication**
(statement 1), under **scaling** (statement 2) and under **inversion and transposition**
(statement 4) — but not under **addition**. Only statement (3) involves a sum of matrices,
which is the signal to look there first.
∴ det(A + B) = det(A) + det(B) is the incorrect statement.

The **order** of the differential equation of a family of curves equals the number of
**independent arbitrary constants** in the family.
**Step 1 — write the family.** A circle of **fixed** radius a, with its centre free to move
anywhere, is
**(x − h)² + (y − k)² = a²**
**Step 2 — count the arbitrary constants.** The radius a is **given**, so it is not
arbitrary. The free quantities are the two coordinates of the centre:
**h** and **k** — that is **2** arbitrary constants
**Step 3 — conclude.** The differential equation therefore has order **2** ✓
**Eliminating h and k explicitly**, to confirm. Differentiating the circle once:
2(x − h) + 2(y − k)y′ = 0
**(x − h) + (y − k)y′ = 0**
Differentiating again:
1 + (y′)² + (y − k)y″ = 0
so
**y − k = −[1 + (y′)²]/y″**
and from the first derivative
**x − h = −(y − k)y′ = y′[1 + (y′)²]/y″**
Substituting both into the original circle:
[1 + (y′)²]²(y′)²/(y″)² + [1 + (y′)²]²/(y″)² = a²
[1 + (y′)²]²[(y′)² + 1]/(y″)² = a²
**[1 + (y′)²]³ = a²(y″)²**
The highest derivative is **y″**, so the order is **2** ✓ — and h and k have both vanished,
confirming that two constants needed two differentiations.
**The variation worth noting.** If the radius were **also** arbitrary, the family would be
all circles, with **three** constants h, k, a, and the order would be **3** — option (4).
The single word "**given**" in "of given radius a" is what makes the answer 2 rather than
3, and it is the whole content of the question.
**A related count.** All straight lines y = mx + c have two constants, hence order 2
(y″ = 0); all circles through the origin have two; all parabolas y² = 4a(x − h) have two.
Counting the genuinely free parameters is always the first move.
∴ 2.

The **degree** of a differential equation is the power of the **highest-order** derivative,
once the equation has been made polynomial in all its derivatives.
**Step 1 — identify the highest-order derivative.** The equation
[1 + (dy/dx)²]² = d²y/dx²
contains dy/dx (order 1) and d²y/dx² (order 2). The highest order is **2**, so the degree
is the power of **d²y/dx²**.
**Step 2 — check the equation is polynomial in its derivatives.** There are no radicals, no
fractional powers, and no derivative inside a sine, logarithm or exponential — both sides
are already polynomial ✓ so the degree is defined and no rearrangement is needed.
**Step 3 — read off the power of d²y/dx².** It appears to the **first** power:
**degree = 1** ✓
**The trap.** The visible **square** on the left tempts the answer 2, and expanding
[1 + (dy/dx)²]² = 1 + 2(dy/dx)² + (dy/dx)⁴ produces a fourth power, tempting the answer 4.
Neither is relevant: the degree is governed **only** by the highest-order derivative, and
the powers of lower-order derivatives count for nothing at all.
So however complicated the dy/dx terms become, if d²y/dx² appears to the first power the
degree is **1**.
**A reminder of the definitions, which are easy to swap.**
**order** = the order of the highest derivative present → here **2**
**degree** = the power of that highest derivative → here **1**
**Where this equation comes from.** Rearranged as y″/[1 + (y′)²]^(3/2) = 1/[1 + (y′)²]^(1/2),
it is close to the formula for the **radius of curvature**, which is why equations of this
shape appear so often in the chapter.
**When the degree would be undefined.** Had the equation contained something like
sin(dy/dx) or log(d²y/dx²), no amount of raising to powers could make it polynomial in the
derivatives, and the degree would **not exist**. That is a standard companion question, and
the contrast is what both are testing.
∴ 1.

An integrating factor is defined only for an equation in **standard linear form**, so the
first move is to divide through by the coefficient of dy/dx.
**Step 1 — put the equation in standard form.** Starting from
x(dy/dx) + 2y = x²
divide every term by x (allowed, since x ≠ 0 is given):
**dy/dx + (2/x)y = x**
Comparing with dy/dx + Py = Q:
**P = 2/x** and **Q = x**
**Step 2 — compute the integrating factor.**
IF = e^(∫P dx)
= e^(∫(2/x)dx)
= e^(2 log|x|)
**Step 3 — simplify the exponent.** Using a log b = log(bᵃ):
2 log|x| = log(x²)
so
IF = e^(log x²) = **x²** ✓
since e and log are inverse functions.
**Check that it works.** Multiplying the standard form by x²:
x²(dy/dx) + 2xy = x³
and the left side is exactly **d(x²y)/dx**, by the product rule ✓ — which is what an
integrating factor is for. Integrating both sides:
x²y = x⁴/4 + C
**y = x²/4 + C/x²**
**Verifying the solution.** dy/dx = x/2 − 2C/x³, so
x(dy/dx) + 2y = x²/2 − 2C/x² + x²/2 + 2C/x² = **x²** ✓ the original equation.
**The commonest error.** Reading P off the equation **before** dividing by x gives P = 2
and IF = e^(2x) ✗ The standard form requires the coefficient of dy/dx to be exactly **1**,
and skipping that division is the single most frequent slip in this topic.
**On the options.** Option (C), e^(log x), simplifies to just **x**, which would be the
integrating factor if P were 1/x. Option (B), log|x|, is the **integral** ∫(1/x)dx rather
than the exponential of it, and option (D) is x rather than x².
∴ x².
